activity_context.topic_title: Calculating Limits of Radical Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

feedback.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=3$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-3x}{\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7}} & =\frac{{3}^{2}-3(3)}{\sqrt{3+4}-\sqrt{7}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-3x}{\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7}} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)}{\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7})(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{x+4})^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{x+4-7} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{x-3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}x(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7}) \\  & =3(\sqrt{3+4}+\sqrt{7}) \\  & =3(2\sqrt{7}) \\  & =6\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$
